title: Jonah and the Bell
premise: August Voss hosts a late-night radio show in the drowned village of Marrow's End, where callers who died the previous week still phone in, calm and conversational. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 rings again across the water, August discovers he is the last living heir of the Voss family who cast it — and the bell remembers its makers. The bell sings a hymn whose final verse was never written down; anyone who hears the whole song must sing along, and those who sing are taken into the metal. Guided by his dead grandmother's voice on the radio and a mute girl who survived the 1911 casting as a child, August must learn the last verse without ever letting it pass his lips. In the flooded belfry he finds his own name already engraved inside the bell, dated next week — and he breaks the song instead of finishing it, shattering the bell and freeing the singers, at the cost of his voice and his place among the living memories of the village.
about_author: Oscar Eastwick is the pen name of a former night-shift radio engineer from coastal East Anglia who spent years maintaining transmitters nobody admitted still received signals. He writes horror about small communities, old machinery, and the things frequencies carry after their owners are gone.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV August. On his late-night show, August takes a call from Mrs. Halloway, who mentions her own funeral with cheerful detail; he checks the obituaries and confirms she died Tuesday. The emotional beat is quiet dread beneath professional routine, establishing the village's strange normalcy.

chapters.title: The Counted Doors
chapters.summary: POV August. We learn his rituals: lights kept burning, doors counted twice nightly, inherited from a grandmother he barely remembers. A listener calls to warn him: 'When the bell rings, don't learn the words.' Beat: unease sharpening into personal stakes.

chapters.title: What the Water Keeps
chapters.summary: POV August. August visits the drowned church ruins at the reservoir's edge, where the 1911 flood took the old quarter. The steeple tip breaks the surface like a tooth. He feels watched. Beat: the past made physical, the village's guilt surfacing.

chapters.title: A Ring With No Bell
chapters.summary: POV August. At 3:11 a.m., every radio in the village plays a low bronze tone though nothing is broadcasting. Windows hum. Dogs go silent. August's studio clock stops. Beat: inciting horror — the impossible made audible.

chapters.title: The Melted Year
chapters.summary: POV August, with archive interludes. In the parish records office, August learns the bell was recast in 1911 from scrap donated by villagers — each family gave metal, including a Voss crucifix. The foundry ledger lists names; his grandfather's line is underlined. Beat: inheritance revealed as obligation.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: POV August. The dead callers grow urgent, overlapping on air, all humming fragments of one hymn. Mrs. Halloway warns him the song has four verses and 'the fifth is being written now.' Beat: escalation; the dead are not malicious but afraid.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Would Not Sing
chapters.summary: POV August. August meets Ida Marsh, ninety-nine, mute since 1911, who communicates by chalkboard. She writes: I HEARD THE WHOLE SONG ONCE. I KEPT MY MOUTH SHUT. IT TOOK MY VOICE INSTEAD. Beat: hope with a terrible price attached.

chapters.title: Verse One
chapters.summary: POV August. The bell rings fully for the first time, audible across the reservoir, and everyone who hears verse one hums it involuntarily for days. August wakes with the melody in his teeth. Beat: contamination — the song gets inside you.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Frequency
chapters.summary: POV August. Between stations, August's radio finds a woman's voice: his grandmother Edith, dead thirty years, singing harmony she shouldn't know. She tells him the Voss family cast themselves into the bell willingly, once, to hold something back. Beat: family history reframed as sacrifice.

chapters.title: What It Holds Back
chapters.summary: POV August, with Edith's radio monologue. Edith explains: the 1911 flood wasn't an accident. The village drowned its own quarter to bury something the bell had woken, and the bell's song keeps it asleep. Stopping the song wakes it. Finishing it feeds it. Beat: the trap closes — no safe option.

chapters.title: The Congregation of the Drowned
chapters.summary: POV August. Villagers begin sleepwalking toward the reservoir at night, standing in the shallows, mouths moving. August pulls a neighbor out; the man thanks him, then returns the next night. Beat: communal dread; isolation of the protagonist.

chapters.title: Ida's Silence
chapters.summary: POV Ida (first time). Flashback to 1911: young Ida in the foundry, watching molten bronze poured, hearing the unfinished hymn rise from the cooling metal. Her father sang along. She never spoke again. Beat: the cost of survival, compassionately rendered.

chapters.title: Verse Two
chapters.summary: POV August. The second verse arrives through the dead callers, sung in unison on air before August can cut the feed. Half the village now carries it. His producer, Ruth, starts humming at her desk, eyes wet. Beat: guilt — August's show is spreading it.

chapters.title: Off Air
chapters.summary: POV Ruth. August takes the station off the air to stop transmission; the council forces him back on, claiming emergency broadcasts. That night the bell rings louder than ever, and Ruth dreams of walking into the water holding a microphone. Beat: institutions fail; the horror adapts.

chapters.title: The Engraving
chapters.summary: POV August. Diving the flooded nave with Ida's nephew, August finds the sunken bell itself, intact, green with century-old silt. Inside the crown, fresh-cut letters read AUGUST VOSS, with a date eight days away. Beat: confrontation with fate; terror becomes intimate.

chapters.title: Verse Three and Four
chapters.summary: POV August. Over two nights the third and fourth verses ring out. The sleepwalkers now stand chest-deep, singing. Edith's voice frays on the radio: 'They're almost done writing the last one, love. It needs a Voss mouth to finish.' Beat: the mechanism understood — the bell wants an heir.

chapters.title: The Fifth Verse, Unwritten
chapters.summary: POV Ida. Ida reveals what she has never told anyone: the fifth verse isn't missing — it's a question the bell asks, and only a blood heir can answer it aloud. Whoever answers completes the song and joins the bronze. Whoever refuses... she doesn't finish the sentence. Beat: the choice named.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for the End
chapters.summary: POV August. August and Ida work to learn the fifth verse's shape without words — its rhythm, its silences — so he can face it knowing what he must not say. Ruth leaves town; half the congregation stands waist-deep now. Beat: grim preparation, tenderness between August and Ida.

chapters.title: The Night of the Date
chapters.summary: POV August. The engraved date arrives. The bell tolls continuously; the water level drops as if the reservoir is inhaling. August walks into the drowned church as the whole village watches from the shore, singing verses one through four. Beat: descent; courage as ritual.

chapters.title: Inside the Bronze
chapters.summary: POV August. In the belfry, the bell shows him the singers within — generations of Vosses, including Edith, holding the sleeping thing below shut like a lid held down from inside. The fifth verse rises in him, complete, irresistible. Beat: climax begins; temptation at full strength.

chapters.title: Breaking the Song
chapters.summary: POV August and Ida. Instead of finishing, August screams the verse backward — sound without meaning, a Voss mouth used against the bell — while Ida, giving back her stolen voice for one word, shouts 'NO' in unison. The hymn snaps. The bell cracks. The thing below stays drowned; the singers dissolve into light on the water. Beat: climax and release.

chapters.title: Silence, Counted Twice
chapters.summary: POV August, epilogue weeks later. August has lost his singing voice and most of his hearing in one ear; the radio show ends with honest static and no callers. The doors are still counted, the lights still on. On quiet nights he thinks he hears one soft note from the water — and lets it go unanswered. Beat: bittersweet resolution; memory kept, identity remade.
